habitat:cabin.headline: Cabin air is where NASA's fire data is richest

sentences.text: In spacecraft cabin air, the FLEX model gives a methanol droplet flame a 72% chance of putting itself out (90% interval 56%–86%), and this input sits inside the flown ISS tests.
Heptane, a heavier fuel, puts itself out less often: 44% (90% interval 30%–59%).
FLEX (99.7), BASS (94.3) and ACME CFI-G (92.1) are the most relevant investigations, and FLEX alone has about 109.1 test-equivalents near this air.
Even here the solid-material record is thin and dominated by one plastic, so cabin fabrics and other polymers still need flight data.

habitat:eva_prep.headline: Raising oxygen to 26.5% already changes how fires behave

sentences.text: At 26.5% O2 and 10.2 psi, the FLEX model gives a methanol droplet flame a 21% chance of putting itself out (90% interval 8%–37%), against 72% in cabin air.
For heptane the chance drops to 7%, so a fire in this atmosphere should be expected to keep burning until it is detected and suppressed.
FLEX is by far the most relevant investigation here (99.2 out of 100), with about 36.8 test-equivalents near this atmosphere.
The most informative next flight test is a methanol droplet at 27% O2, 0.60 atm and 30% CO2, where the model is still uncertain (90% interval 10%–51%).

habitat:moon_base.headline: In lunar-base air, fires stop putting themselves out, and the data runs thin

sentences.text: In lunar-base air (30% O2 at 10.2 psi), the FLEX model gives a methanol droplet flame only a 6% chance of putting itself out (90% interval 2%–14%), against 72% in spacecraft cabin air.
Only 37 of 1,613 flight records with a known atmosphere sit inside the lunar-base envelope, and no solid material has been burned there.
FLEX is the most relevant investigation (95.1 out of 100), followed by ACME CFI-G (66.8) and ACME BRE (48.1).
Material screening done at 21% / 1 atm cannot be carried over without re-testing, and the highest-value next flight experiment is solid-material flammability at ≥30% O₂ and ≤10.2 psi.

habitat:exploration.headline: The exploration atmosphere sits beyond NASA's flown droplet tests

sentences.text: At 34% O2 and 8.2 psi, the FLEX model estimates only a 1% chance that a methanol droplet flame puts itself out (90% interval 0%–4%), but this is an extrapolation: no FLEX test was flown at such a low pressure.
ACME CFI-G (86.0 out of 100) and FLEX (82.3) are the closest evidence, and ACME CFI-G has about 16.4 test-equivalents near this atmosphere.
Above 30% O₂, flames stop putting themselves out, so a fire here has to be detected and actively suppressed.
No solid-material test has been flown inside the lunar-base envelope, so cabin materials for this atmosphere still need flight data.

habitat:suit.headline: Spacesuit oxygen is outside all flight data

sentences.text: For a spacesuit (100% O2 at 4.3 psi), Skylab Phoenix withholds any prediction: the atmosphere sits 14.3 units from the nearest flown FLEX test, more than twice the out-of-data limit of 1.33.
Even the most relevant investigation, FLEX, scores only 49.7 out of 100 here, with essentially no tests near this atmosphere.
Suit fire safety therefore cannot be read from the cabin experiments in PSI; it needs dedicated tests in pure oxygen at low pressure.
FLEX burned single fuel droplets on the ISS to map when liquid-fuel flames go out and how well gaseous suppressants such as CO2 and helium work.

All 274 tests have a labeled outcome across 12%–34% O2 and 0.69–3.05 atm, which makes FLEX the most relevant investigation for the lunar base (rank 1 of 24) and the backbone of Skylab Phoenix's model.
ACME CFI-G burned gas flames in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack to find when cool diffusion flames appear for propane, n-butane and n-pentane.
Its 333 labeled tests reach 12%–85% O2 and 0.49–3.27 atm, so it is the closest evidence for the exploration atmosphere (86.0 out of 100) and ranks 2 of 24 for the lunar base.
ACME BRE used a gas burner that emulates burning solids to describe fires in still microgravity air in terms of material properties.

Burning stayed steady for emulated materials such as PMMA and nylon even with no airflow, which questions the usual step of cutting ventilation to fight a spacecraft fire; it ranks 3 of 24 for the lunar base.
BASS burned solid samples in a fan-driven flow duct on the ISS to bridge NASA's 1 g material screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) and real flammability in microgravity.
Its 121 records (59 with a labeled outcome) were run between 15.9% and 22.7% O2 at cabin pressure, so it is highly relevant for the cabin (94.3) but less so for the lunar base (47.4).
BASS-II extended BASS to study ignition, flame spread and extinction of solid fuels in low-speed forced flows, the regime of a ventilated cabin.
Its 128 records cover only 13.6%–22.2% O2, so it scores 90.9 for the cabin but 42.1 for the lunar base, whose oxygen level it never reached.
ACME Flame Design studied spherical normal and inverse diffusion flames of ethylene and methane to find when they start producing soot.
Its 327 records reach 19.8%–85.0% O2 and 0.43–3.02 atm, but none carries a fire-safety outcome label, so it ranks 6 of 24 for the lunar base.
SAME-R measured how big smoke particles grow in microgravity and how that depends on how the smoke was made and carried.
Its 109 records were all run in cabin air (21% O2), so it matters for detector design in the cabin (80.0) but says little about oxygen-enriched habitats (31.7 for the lunar base).
Saffire-II burned large material samples inside a Cygnus cargo spacecraft to see how fast a realistic fire grows and how low-g flammability limits compare with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.
Its 9 samples were burned at 21.5%–22.1% O2 and the same materials were also burned on the ground, a rare side-by-side comparison of microgravity and Earth gravity.
Saffire-I studied how fast a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compared low-g flammability limits with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.
Its 2 burns, at 21.5% O2 with the airflow in opposite directions, show that flow direction is a design variable for cabin ventilation.
SAME measured the size of smoke particles from spacecraft materials in microgravity to judge whether existing smoke detectors would see them.
Its 8 records were all run in cabin air (21% O2), and together with SAME-R (similarity 0.72) it is the main PSI evidence for fire detection.
Saffire-III repeated the large-scale fire test of Saffire-I to see how quickly a fire grows in low gravity.
PSI holds only 2 records for it and no oxygen level per test, so its relevance is the same for every habitat (30.0 out of 100).
ACME E-FIELD studied how electric fields change gas flames, their ion currents and their soot.
Its 230 records were run in cabin air and the study was not aimed at space fire safety, so it ranks 12 of 24 for the lunar base.
DAFT and DAFT-2 checked that a commercial particle counter would work in microgravity before SAME relied on it to measure smoke.
It holds 2 records and ranks 13 of 24 for the lunar base, but it underpins the detection evidence of SAME (similarity 0.60).
SPICE burned gas jets in a fan-driven flow duct on the ISS to find the smoke point, where a flame starts releasing soot.
Its 435 records were run in cabin air (21% O2), which makes it relevant for the cabin (65.0) and EVA prep (60.0) but not for the exploration atmosphere (15.0).
ACME s-Flame studied spherical diffusion flames, with and without soot, to test detailed computer models of flame chemistry and transport.
Its 276 records span 21%–30% O2, but without outcome labels it ranks 15 of 24 for the lunar base.
CFI burned n-dodecane droplets in the ISS droplet rig to study cool flames at pressures from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
Its 79 records cover 17%–21% O2 and 0.50–5.00 atm, and in the archive it is closest to FLEX (similarity 0.58).
ACME CLD studied weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene at the extremes of fuel dilution to test computer models.
Its 344 records were run in cabin air (21% O2), so it ranks 17 of 24 for the lunar base.
SLICE studied the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity, including when they lift off the burner.
Its 12 records were run in cabin air (21% O2); its closest relative is SPICE (similarity 0.70), and it ranks 18 of 24 for the lunar base.
FLEX-2 extended FLEX to fuels and conditions closer to real combustors, including two-component droplets.
PSI holds only 8 records for it, without conditions per test, so it scores 15.0 for every habitat even though 48 publications are listed.
This ground study used FLEX flight data, new simulations and counterflow flames to map how cool flames turn into hot flames and go out.
Its 8 summary records are analysis results rather than flight tests, so it ranks 20 of 24 for the lunar base.
This ground study built and validated new computer models of concurrent flame spread over solids in microgravity, checked against BASS.
It has no data table in PSI (rank 21 of 24 for the lunar base), but it gives tools to predict the flammability limits of new materials.
This ground study combined simulations and experiments to explain the large difference in soot formation between 1g and 0g flames.
It has no data table in PSI and ranks 22 of 24 for the lunar base.
This ground study used FLEX flight data and multi-physics simulations to see how heat and airflow disturbances decide the fate of a droplet cool flame.
It has no data table in PSI (rank 23 of 24 for the lunar base), but its models aim at safer operating envelopes for spacecraft.
This ground study simulated smoke from heated materials to quantify how gravity changes smoke particle growth.
It has no data table in PSI and ranks 24 of 24 for the lunar base, but it supports better smoke detectors together with SAME (similarity 0.40).
